title: Competitors Coexist When Each Limits Itself More

scenes.tts: On a rocky shore at Millport in Scotland, one barnacle lives high on the rock. Another covers the rock below. Joseph Connell removed the lower one, Balanus, from around the upper one, Chthamalus. Then Chthamalus survived well in the zone it normally lacks. What had held it back? Connell saw Balanus smother, undercut and crush its neighbour.
scenes.visual: Two barnacle bands on a shore; Balanus removed around Chthamalus; Chthamalus stays; ghost arrows show crowding
scenes.narration: On a rocky shore at Millport in Scotland, one barnacle lives high on the rock. Another covers the rock below. Joseph Connell removed the lower one, Balanus, from around the upper one, Chthamalus. Then Chthamalus survived well in the zone it normally lacks. What had held it back? Connell saw Balanus smother, undercut and crush its neighbour.

scenes.tts: That is competition. Individuals use a resource in short supply, so each lowers the survival, growth or reproduction of the others. The Lotka Volterra model asks when two competitors can live together. Each species is slowed by its own numbers, up to its carrying capacity, big K. It is also slowed by the other species, counted in its own units. Alpha one two is the effect of one species two individual on species one. If alpha one two is one half, two species two individuals crowd species one as much as one of its own.

scenes.tts: Take values invented for practice. Big K is one hundred for species one, and eighty for species two. Both alphas are one half. With twenty of each, species one grows by seven individuals per day. Now draw each isocline, the line where one species stops growing. Species one stops on a line from one hundred on its own axis to two hundred on the other. Species two stops on a line from eighty to one hundred sixty. They cross at eighty and forty.
scenes.caption: Take values invented for practice. K is 100 for species 1, and 80 for species 2. Both alphas are 0.5. With 20 of each, species 1 grows by 7 individuals per day. Now draw each isocline, the line where one species stops growing. Species 1 stops on a line from 100 on its own axis to 200 on the other. Species 2 stops on a line from 80 to 160. They cross at 80 and 40.
scenes.visual: Axes; the two isoclines draw and cross at 80 and 40
scenes.narration: Take values invented for practice. K is 100 for species 1, and 80 for species 2. Both alphas are 0.5. With 20 of each, species 1 grows by 7 individuals per day. Now draw each isocline, the line where one species stops growing. Species 1 stops on a line from 100 on its own axis to 200 on the other. Species 2 stops on a line from 80 to 160. They cross at 80 and 40.

scenes.tts: Is that crossing stable? Let each species start rare. Species one, rare among species two at its carrying capacity, grows by point three per day. Species two, rare among species one at one hundred, grows by point zero nine four per day. Each can increase when rare. So in this sketch, the model predicts stable coexistence at eighty and forty.
scenes.caption: Is that crossing stable? Let each species start rare. Species 1, rare among species 2 at its carrying capacity, grows by 0.3 per day. Species 2, rare among species 1 at 100, grows by 0.094 per day. Each can increase when rare. So in this sketch, the model predicts stable coexistence at 80 and 40.
scenes.visual: Rare-invader arrows on both axes point into the plot; a computed path from 20,20 settles at the crossing
scenes.narration: Is that crossing stable? Let each species start rare. Species 1, rare among species 2 at its carrying capacity, grows by 0.3 per day. Species 2, rare among species 1 at 100, grows by 0.094 per day. Each can increase when rare. So in this sketch, the model predicts stable coexistence at 80 and 40.

scenes.tts: Now change one coefficient. Raise alpha two one to one. Species two, rare among species one at one hundred, now has a growth rate of minus point zero six two five per day. It cannot get started, while species one still can. The model predicts that species one excludes species two.
scenes.caption: Now change one coefficient. Raise α₂₁ to 1. Species 2, rare among species 1 at 100, now has a growth rate of −0.0625 per day. It cannot get started, while species 1 still can. The model predicts that species 1 excludes species 2.
scenes.visual: Species 2 isocline swings down; rare-species 2 arrow turns red; the path ends with species 2 at zero
scenes.narration: Now change one coefficient. Raise α₂₁ to 1. Species 2, rare among species 1 at 100, now has a growth rate of −0.0625 per day. It cannot get started, while species 1 still can. The model predicts that species 1 excludes species 2.

scenes.tts: Both outcomes came from two conditions. Species one needs K one above alpha one two K two. Species two needs K two above alpha two one K one. The growth rate never appears in them, so the fastest grower need not win. Keep the rule: in this model, competitors coexist when each limits itself more than it limits the other.
